title: Calories
objective: After this level you can explain what a calorie measures.
summary: A calorie is a unit of energy; the food Calorie is a kilocalorie. Atwater's room-sized calorimeter showed energy is conserved in people. How much energy a body uses varies from person to person.

cards.headline: A calorie is a unit, like a meter.
cards.body: It measures energy, the way a meter measures length. It isn't a score or a verdict on a food. So what exactly does it measure, and how did anyone measure the energy a person uses?

cards.headline: Warming a gram of water
cards.body: One calorie is the heat it takes to warm 1 gram of water by 1 °C. That's tiny, so food labels use a bigger unit: the Calorie with a capital C, which is a kilocalorie, 1,000 small calories. When food is broken down, its energy is released, and your cells spend it on everything they do, from building proteins on up.

cards.headline: A room built to measure people
cards.body: In 1896 at Wesleyan University, Wilbur Atwater's team began about 500 experiments in a respiration calorimeter: a small sealed room where volunteers stayed, sometimes for days, while the heat and carbon dioxide they gave off were measured. It showed that the law of conservation of energy holds for people too, and let the team work out the energy in foods: about 4 Calories per gram for protein or carbohydrate, about 9 for fat.

cards.headline: Every body runs its own budget
cards.body: How much energy a body uses isn't one number. It varies with age, sex, body size, physical activity and each person's metabolic rate, so no single figure fits everyone. Much of it goes on work you never notice. Your brain is about 2 percent of an adult's body weight but uses about 20 percent of the body's calories, at a fairly steady rate whether you're solving puzzles or daydreaming.
